items.followUp: Define vectors and give two examples.

rubric.why: A scalar is distinguished from a vector by having magnitude but no direction.
rubric.description: Defines a scalar as a quantity with magnitude only and no direction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it has magnitude but no direction.

rubric.why: The examples must be scalar quantities.
rubric.description: Gives two valid examples of scalar quantities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two correct examples.

modelAnswer: A scalar is a physical quantity that has magnitude only and no direction.

items.followUp: Differentiate between translatory motion and rotatory motion.

rubric.why: Rotatory motion is motion about the body's own axis.
rubric.description: States that in rotatory motion a body turns about its own axis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying rotation about the body's own axis.

rubric.why: Circular motion describes motion along a circular path about a centre or axis.
rubric.description: States that in circular motion a body moves along a circular path about a point or axis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying motion along a circular path.

modelAnswer: In rotatory motion, a body turns about its own axis; for example, a rotating fan.
In circular motion, a body moves along a circular path around a point or axis; for example, the Moon moves around the Earth.

items.followUp: What is sliding friction? How does it compare with rolling friction?

rubric.why: Rolling friction occurs when an object rolls over a surface.
rubric.description: Identifies rolling friction as friction acting when an object rolls over a surface.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking rolling friction with a rolling object and surface.

rubric.why: Sliding friction acts when surfaces slide over one another and is generally greater than rolling friction.
rubric.description: Identifies sliding friction and states that rolling friction is smaller than sliding friction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the distinction and their relative sizes.

modelAnswer: Rolling friction acts when an object rolls over a surface.
Sliding friction acts when one surface slides over another; sliding friction is greater than rolling friction.

items.followUp: What is the moment of a force? State its S.I. unit.

rubric.why: A couple consists of two equal, opposite, parallel forces.
rubric.description: Defines a couple as two equal, opposite, parallel forces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the force characteristics.

rubric.why: The separated forces produce rotation, and a suitable example completes the answer.
rubric.description: States that the forces act along different lines to produce rotation and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the turning effect and a valid example.

modelAnswer: A couple is a pair of equal, opposite, parallel forces acting along different lines, which produces rotation.
Turning a steering wheel is an example of the action of a couple.

items.followUp: Define stable equilibrium and give an example.

rubric.why: In neutral equilibrium, displacement does not change the height of the centre of gravity.
rubric.description: Defines neutral equilibrium in terms of the centre of gravity remaining at the same height when displaced.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that displacement leaves the centre of gravity at the same height.

rubric.why: A ball or marble on a level surface is a standard example.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of neutral equilibrium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an example such as a ball on a horizontal surface.

modelAnswer: A body is in neutral equilibrium if, when displaced, the height of its centre of gravity remains unchanged.
A ball on a horizontal surface is an example.

items.followUp: Define pressure, write its formula and give its S.I. unit.

rubric.why: Density is defined as mass per unit volume.
rubric.description: Defines density as mass per unit volume.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct definition.

rubric.why: The formula and S.I. unit express density in standard form.
rubric.description: Gives the formula and the S.I. unit of density.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula and unit.

modelAnswer: Density is the mass per unit volume of a substance.
Density = mass / volume, or ρ = m / V.
The S.I. unit of density is kg/m³.

items.followUp: State Hooke's law and explain what happens when the elastic limit is exceeded.

rubric.why: Hooke's law relates extension to applied force while the elastic limit is not exceeded.
rubric.description: States that extension is directly proportional to applied force, provided the elastic limit is not exceeded.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the proportionality and its condition.

rubric.why: The elastic limit is the boundary beyond which the body no longer fully returns to its original shape after the force is removed.
rubric.description: Explains the meaning of elastic limit in terms of recovery of the original shape.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct explanation of the limit.

modelAnswer: Hooke's law states that extension is directly proportional to the applied force, provided the elastic limit is not exceeded.
The elastic limit is the maximum limit up to which a body returns to its original shape when the deforming force is removed.

items.followUp: What are the fixed points used to graduate a Celsius thermometer?

rubric.why: The lower fixed point is the ice point, 0°C at standard atmospheric pressure.
rubric.description: Identifies the lower fixed point as the ice point at 0°C.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct point and temperature.

rubric.why: The upper fixed point is the steam point, 100°C at standard atmospheric pressure.
rubric.description: Identifies the upper fixed point as the steam point at 100°C.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct point and temperature.

modelAnswer: The lower fixed point is the temperature of melting ice, 0°C at standard atmospheric pressure.
The upper fixed point is the temperature of steam above boiling water, 100°C at standard atmospheric pressure.
